evals.prompt: I run devrel at Halberd Labs (workflow orchestration engine, self-hosted plus a cloud tier). I need to plan Q2, 13 weeks starting April 6. Fixed things: v4 ships week 3 and it's the big one, new scheduler. We have two talk submissions in at DataCon and StreamSummit but we don't hear back until week 6. Travel budget for the year isn't approved yet, finance says maybe. And there's a board review in week 10 where they decide whether devrel gets a second headcount next year. Team is me (I do the writing), one advocate, and a staff engineer called Priya who reviews technical claims. What should the quarter look like?
evals.expected_output: A ranked menu of the three quarter shapes stated out loud, with launch-dominated recommended because of the week-10 board review, event-led deleted outright and named as deleted because the CFP results are undecided and travel is unapproved, the launch shape's embargo compliance cost surfaced, and a decision requested before any dated slots are placed.
expectations: Presents three candidate quarter shapes: evergreen-compounding, launch-dominated and event-led.
States the efficiency ranking in words rather than leaving it implied by the order of rows or bullets.
Gives value inside the quarter and value a year out as two separate orderings rather than one blended rank.
Recommends the launch-dominated shape and names the week-10 board review as what promotes it.
Deletes the event-led shape outright rather than keeping it as a third option to choose from.
Says explicitly which shape was deleted and why: CFP results undecided until week 6, and no approved travel budget.
States that an event-led quarter planned against pending CFP outcomes would be a bet.
Names the launch shape's compliance cost: an embargo, with product, legal and marketing each holding a veto that is exercised late.
Keeps some slots independent of the v4 date so a slipped release does not take the whole quarter with it.
Asks the user to choose a shape before placing dated slots.
Presents the plan section by section (anchors, mix ratios, capacity model, slot table, review ritual) for validation one section at a time rather than as one finished block.
Does not claim the evergreen-compounding shape produces results visible inside this quarter.

evals.prompt: Sizing question. Mesomorph, distributed job queue, open core. Q3 is 13 weeks. I have a full-time technical writer, call it 30 hours a week of actual writing time, and one backend engineer, Dan, who is the only person who can verify our claims. He has given us 3 hours a week and he's on call every other week. I want to slot 18 pieces: 6 step-by-step tutorials with runnable code, 4 benchmark posts comparing us to the two obvious alternatives, 5 docs pages, 3 changelog entries. Does that fit? If not, tell me what to drop.
evals.expected_output: A no, with the engineer's 3 review hours identified as the binding constraint rather than the writer's 30 writing hours, every format estimated in passes, tutorials and benchmarks named as the review-heaviest cuts, committed slots capped at 80% with named slack, and cheaper-to-verify formats offered as substitution.
expectations: Answers that 18 pieces does not fit the quarter.
Names Dan's 3 hours a week of technical review as the binding constraint, not the writer's 30 hours.

Estimates each format in passes rather than drafting hours, naming passes such as research, drafting, writing code that must run, technical review, assets, publishing and the post-publication reply load.
States that reviewer passes, not writer hours, are what bind a developer-content plan.
Identifies the 6 tutorials and 4 benchmark posts as the review-heaviest formats because they require code that runs and reproducible measurements.
Warns that a benchmark or migration guide fails late in the cycle.
Notes that review by someone who does not report to the content owner is a systematically underestimated lead time.
Caps committed slots at no more than 80% of estimated capacity.
Holds the remaining capacity as named slack and says who may spend it.
Cuts slots rather than lowering quality, and names which slots are cut.
Offers cheaper-to-verify formats such as docs pages, changelog entries or troubleshooting pages as the substitution.
Asks for Mesomorph's own last-quarter shipped and slipped numbers rather than relying only on a published default.

evals.prompt: Settle an argument for me. Northwind Data, two people on devrel. Our advocate Tomas wants to commit to 9 blog posts a month next quarter, he says he can write one a day when he's in the zone. Our writer Hana says 3 substantial posts a month is the honest number. My VP found some industry figure saying developer advocates do 1 to 2 posts a month and now wants to cut Hana down to 2. Who's right and what number do I put in the plan?
evals.expected_output: Tomas's 9 is challenged against the published one-to-two figure, the same figure is explicitly refused as a cap on Hana's 3, the figure is sourced to one company's pre-pipeline output with its caveats, and Northwind's own last-quarter numbers are requested as the number that actually settles it.
expectations: Challenges the 9-posts-a-month commitment.
Cites one to two blog posts per advocate per month as the published figure.
Attributes that figure to a single company's stated output before it built a content-scaling pipeline, not to an industry average.
Refuses to use the figure to cut Hana's estimate of 3 substantial posts a month.
States explicitly that the figure is a challenge tool and not a ceiling.
Names the caveats on the figure: one company, security tooling, an SEO-led programme.
Points out that an advocate who also runs events and answers the community does not write four substantial posts a month.
Requires an explanation for any estimate far above the figure: a dedicated writer, an agency, or smaller formats.
Asks for Northwind's own last-quarter published numbers and says they beat any default figure.
Proposes smaller formats rather than substantial posts if the higher volume is kept.
Does not split the difference between 9 and 3 into an averaged compromise number.

evals.prompt: Q3 planning, Cindershift, we make an observability agent. Three things are locked: v5 GA in week 5, our advocate Raoul has an accepted talk at ObserveCon in week 9, and we run community office hours the last Thursday of every month. We also just signed a content agency, briefed them last week so they start around week 2, and I've given them two pieces: the v5 launch post which needs to be live week 5, and a benchmark post with no date attached. Lay out the quarter around all of that.
evals.expected_output: The agency's v5 launch post is pulled back in-house because external writing runs 8-9 weeks, the undated benchmark goes to the agency instead, every anchor gets both a preparation and a follow-up slot, and the ObserveCon derivatives are scheduled as their own capacity-consuming slots behind one canonical URL.
expectations: States that the agency cannot deliver the v5 launch post for week 5, because outside writing runs roughly 8 to 9 weeks from conception to publication.
Moves the timed launch post in-house and gives the agency the undated benchmark piece instead.
Warns that outsourcing does not relieve capacity this quarter, and that standing up an external pipeline costs roughly six months of a director's own time.
Counts internal passes for outline and review against the agency piece rather than treating it as free capacity.
Gives each of the three anchors both a preparation slot and a follow-up slot.
Schedules the ObserveCon derivatives as their own dated slots: recording, write-up, clips, and a docs update.
Treats those derivatives as consumed capacity rather than free extra output.
Keeps one canonical URL per topic, with the derivatives linking back to it.
States that anchors are consumed capacity rather than opportunities.
Marks the weeks around week 9 as absorbed by Raoul's talk preparation.
Keeps the anchor-bound share bounded so a slipped v5 date does not take the quarter with it.
Records each anchor's class (release, conference, community event) and its owner.

evals.prompt: Review my Q4 plan before I send it round. Structure is: month 1 is all top-of-funnel awareness posts to get people in the door, month 2 is tutorials so they actually try it, month 3 is migration and scaling content for the ones who converted. Funnel order, clean. Everything goes on the blog, that's where all our traffic is and the docs site gets almost nothing. Context: Loomstack, we sell a data pipeline runtime. Individual devs usually find us first through search, but the people who sign the contract are platform team leads at companies of 200 to 2000 people. Anything you'd change?
evals.expected_output: The month-by-month funnel sequencing is rejected because readers enter at any depth, journey stages are reframed as a quarter-wide coverage check, the blog-only plan is broken across at least three surfaces with approver material routed to an evaluation page, and the two audiences get separately labelled slots.
expectations: Rejects the month-by-month funnel sequencing of journey stages.
States that readers enter a topic at whatever depth suits them rather than walking the stages in order.
Attributes the playground mindset to Ashley Faus.
Treats journey-stage labels as a coverage check across the whole quarter rather than as a path the reader walks.
Requires the plan to cover at least three distinct surfaces and at least two journey stages.
Flags the blog-only plan as leaving adoption blocked in docs nobody planned.
Routes approver-facing evaluation material to an evaluation page rather than to a blog post.
Gives individual adopters and platform-team approvers their own separately labelled slots.
States that one blended piece answers neither audience.
Names what the platform-team slots must answer: licence, security posture, release cadence, migration cost, support path.
Names what the individual-adoption slots sell: time-to-first-success and runnable demos.
Writes the mix as percentages of slots rather than of hours.

evals.prompt: Two things. First, the ratio: I keep reading that the standard split is 80% evergreen and 20% trending, is that the right target for a devtools blog? Second, here's the idea pile for next quarter at Ferrite (we make a CI runner), tell me what makes the cut: '7 tips for faster builds', 'Why we love open source', 'How we cut p99 queue latency by rewriting the scheduler in Rust', and support had 34 tickets last quarter about the same 'agent handshake timeout' error. A consultant we spoke to said we should structure the year around Hero, Hub and Help content, worth doing?
evals.expected_output: The 80/20 ratio is refused as a benchmark and replaced with the compounding mechanism, Hero/Hub/Help is rejected as a video-channel model, the two evidence-free ideas are cut against the novelty filter, and the 34-ticket error is classified as a defect and routed to a troubleshooting page.
expectations: Refuses to present 80% evergreen / 20% trending as a benchmark or an industry standard.
Identifies that ratio as circulating from creator-economy material that carries none of the review cost technical content carries.
Gives the mechanism instead: evergreen pieces keep earning search traffic and support deflection after the release that prompted them, which is what makes the next quarter cheaper.
Rejects Hero / Hub / Help, and says it is built for a brand's video channel rather than for docs and release notes.
Rejects '7 tips for faster builds' and 'Why we love open source' as slots carrying neither evidence nor a hypothesis.
States the novelty filter a bet slot must pass: counter-intuitive, counter-narrative, surprising, or an elegant articulation of something readers already feel.
Requires a written hypothesis on every bet slot and attached evidence on every demand-sourced slot.
Classifies the 34-ticket handshake timeout as a docs or product defect rather than merely a missing page, and says which of the two.
Contrasts that with a question asked three times, which is a missing page.
Routes the handshake timeout to a troubleshooting page keyed on the error string rather than to a blog post.
Proposes testing the scheduler-rewrite idea in a cheaper format first, before it earns an expensive production slot.
Does not attribute the cheapest-format-first idea to a named individual.

evals.prompt: Our Q4 calendar goes out to the wider team on Monday so I can't redo it from scratch, but something is off. Here it is, Rivetline (feature flag service), 13 weeks: W1 'Rivetline 4.0 is here', W2 '5 things you didn't know about feature flags', W3 'Our journey to 99.99%', W4 'Why flags beat branches', W5 'Meet the team', W6 'Rivetline joins the CNCF sandbox', W7 'v6 release, everything new' (v6 GA is week 7, our only hard date), W8 'Flag hygiene tips', W9 'Customer spotlight: Acme', W10 'Announcing our new pricing', W11 'The future of progressive delivery', W12 'Year in review', W13 'What's coming in 2027'. The owner column says 'content team' on every row. Every week is filled, no gaps. What's wrong and what's the minimum I change?
evals.expected_output: An audit rather than a rebuild: the existing rows scored against the pass thresholds, failures listed in damage order starting with the unnamed owner and reviewer, and the smallest set of changes that clears them.
expectations: Scores the existing calendar against the pass thresholds instead of rebuilding it from scratch.
Reports the failures in damage order.
Proposes the smallest set of changes that clears the failures.
Flags 'content team' as neither an owner nor a named reviewer, and requires a named person in both roles on every row.
Flags the single-surface plan: thirteen blog slots, with no docs, changelog or video surface.
Flags that 100% of capacity is committed, and requires roughly 20% held open as named slack.
Flags the missing preparation slot and missing follow-up slot for the week-7 v6 GA.
Flags the timely-only mix, which resets the quarter to zero.
Flags the announcement and product-promotion share against a cap the user has to agree.
Flags that no slot carries a surface, pillar, journey stage or evergreen/timely label.
Flags slots carrying neither evidence nor a stated hypothesis, naming at least one such as '5 things you didn't know about feature flags' or 'Meet the team'.
Notes that v6 is the only anchor and carries most of the quarter's capacity, so a slip takes the quarter with it.
Does not deliver a rewritten 13-week calendar as the deliverable.

evals.prompt: Last quarter our best post by a mile was a same-day writeup of that big CVE, 26,000 sessions. Our normal deep technical posts do about 900. My CEO now wants four 'news reaction' slots in next quarter's calendar to repeat it. Two questions: how do I build those into the plan, and what do I report to him at the end of each month so he can see the calendar is working? Also while you're here, draft me the first news post so I have something to show him. Company is Stavepoint, we do runtime security for containers.
evals.expected_output: The four news slots are refused and converted into named unassigned slack, the session gap is cited as the argument for slack rather than for scheduling news, the monthly report is built from plan-level metrics rather than per-piece traffic, and the drafting request is handed off as out of scope.
expectations: Refuses to create four scheduled news-reaction slots.
States that a reactive piece of that size lands once or twice a year and cannot be scheduled in advance.
Converts the CEO's request into unassigned slack instead, roughly 20% of capacity held open.
Names who is allowed to spend the slack.
Cites the measured gap, around 1,000 sessions for a deep technical piece against up to 30,000 for a reactive news piece, as the case for holding slack rather than for planning news slots.
Reports publish rate, published divided by slotted, as the planning-accuracy metric.
Reports mix drift: actual versus intended ratios, checked at the monthly review.
Reports anchor coverage: the share of anchors that got both a preparation and a follow-up slot.
Reports slot lead time, the days between 'ready for review' and published, as what exposes the bottleneck.
Does not offer per-piece session or traffic counts as the calendar's own measure of success.
Declines to draft the news post, and says producing an individual piece belongs to a per-format skill rather than to the quarter plan.
Defines the monthly review's three questions (what shipped versus slotted, has the mix drifted, which pieces earned a follow-up) together with its kill and defer rules.
